Q: asp.net mvc c# with sql without ORM A:

As you mentioned, you can use "classic" SQL commands with ADO.NET. Here is a good example: Using ASP.Net MVC with Classic ADO.Net

Another way, and in my opinion a very fast and convenient way, is to use the Dapper framework. I would recommend you to use Dapper with Stored Procedures. It's a good trade-off between ORM (like Entity Framework) and classical SQL commands.

Q: Merge / convert multiple PDF files into one PDF A:

Considering that pdfunite is part of Poppler, it has a higher chance to be installed. Usage is also simpler than pdftk:

⚠ IMPORTANT: Just make sure you remember to provide out.pdf, or else it will overwrite the last input file in your command ⚠

pdfunite in-1.pdf in-2.pdf in-n.pdf out.pdf

A safer solution may include a test of non-existence, targeting the output file:

export output_file=out.pdf && \
! test -e $output_file && \
pdfunite in-1.pdf in-2.pdf in-n.pdf $output_file

Q: Return smallest time step A:

Getting the smallest timeframe by finding the minimum value of differences divided by defined splits.

Data

dates_d <- seq.Date(1, 14, by = 1)   # days
dates_m <- seq.Date(1, 137, by = 30) # approx. month
dates_x <- seq.Date(1, 543, by = 90) # approx. 3 months

Definitions

splits = c(second = 60, minute = 3660, hour = 14400, day = 86400, week = 86400 * 7,
           month = 86400 * 30, bimonth = 86400 * 30 * 2, quarter = 86400 * 30 * 3,
           season = 86400 * 30 * 5, halfyear = 86400 * 366 / 2, year = 86400 * 366)

Function

smallest_tp <- \(x, ts = splits){ 
  names(which.min(apply(abs(sapply(ts, \(i){ 
    (diff.Date(as.POSIXct(x), units = "secs") / i) - 1 } )), 2, min)))
  }

output

smallest_tp(c(dates_x, dates_d))
[1] "day"

smallest_tp(c(dates_x, dates_m))
[1] "month"

smallest_tp(dates_x)
[1] "quarter"

Q: Best fine-tuning method A:

You'll deal with Catastrophic Forgetting.

The sad reality is that fine tuning always has a cost. That cost is... general intelligence.

https://huggingface.co/collections/nvidia/nemotron-post-training-v3 is an example of a company who have released a model and the full dataset that they have used to train their model (their entire post-training dataset).

I wouldn't recommend nemotron 3 super, it's Nvidia's best model, but it's no good. However, your only capability to train your data truly into the model is to mix your data randomly together with the actual full post-training dataset used to train the model.

Every GPU-hour you spend post training or fine tune your model on narrow data is an hour where your model becomes less intelligent, more confused, and it never truly learns what you're training it on. That might be a viable solution for affecting response format? But even then you're dealing with catastrophic forgetting by the minute.

Post training is definitely not a strategy to have an LLM learn any new information in a general sense.

If you want to

improve performance, handle edge cases, and ensure better generalization across tasks and domains.

Then you have exactly one option- pay Mistral AI to train a model taking into account your own dataset, and randomizing it together with their dataset. And this is not an advertisement. They're the only company I know of that even offers a service of real fine tuning. I'm talking about fine turning that actually works. I am not affiliated BTW, and I would never recommend anyone to go through that process.

You're much better off relying on in-context learning rather than fine-tuning. Especially since new architectures such as Qwen's HybridAttention, and TurboQuant allow to fit 152,000 tokens of context Easily on an RTX 5090 32 GiB GPU.

In-context learning is what LLMs and the attention mechanism have been designed to be good at. Fine-turning has never worked, ever. A fine tuned model is always less general, less capable than the original. Unless you yourself have a post-training dataset that beats the original company's in generality, quality and scale. Or unless it's a company like Nvidia who release their dataset for you to randomize your own data into.

In that case you would be performing a full, proper post-training with randomized data. This way the model always preserves its incentive to keep its own general knowledge and capabilities- it's constantly being tested up until the very last token it's being trained on!

Q: QML ChartView : mapToValue not taking very exactly? A:

The issue is not with mapToValue, but your axes

This becomes apparent, when I add the following line of code:

Component.onCompleted: axes[0].labelFormat = "%2.5f"

Note, how your X-Axis values slightly change. The reason is, that the default axis that is generated for your chart will follow the concept:

  • min value: 0
  • max value: 4.1 (your line ending)
  • tick count: 5, evenly distributed
  • Format: one digit numerical value

In other words: The default axis will split the values into four equally wide segments with five ticks. The axis values are then displayed, rounded to the first digit.

Because your maximum value is 4.1, your axis labels are actually at [0, 1.025, 2.05, 3.075, 4.1], which get rounded to display [0, 1.0, 2.0, 3.1, 4.1]. Your mouse hover is (more) exact, and therefor reveals the inaccuracy.

To resolve this issue, you will need to adapt your axis to your needs. There are multiple ways to do that, I'll show you a few:

1. A more detailed axis label

As shown above, you can add

Component.onCompleted: axes[0].labelFormat = "%2.5f"

To add the number of digits displayed for your axis values, making them show up less misleading

2. Set the ticks to more intuitive values

Instead of letting the axis auto-define tick values, you can define a tick scale that fits your needs (Available since QtCharts 2.3):

Component.onCompleted: {
  axes[0].tickAnchor = 0
  axes[0].tickInterval = 1
  axes[0].tickType = ValueAxis.TicksDynamic
}

Note, how in this variant the ticks do not fall exactly on the graphs right edge, since they are drawn at the exact integer values of the scale.

3. Add a dedicated ValueAxis Instance

Instead of manipulating the default axis at completion, you can declare your own axis items to specify your axis design:

ChartView {
  id: chartView
  
  ValueAxis {
    id: xAxis
    tickAnchor: 0
    tickInterval: 1
    tickType: ValueAxis.TicksDynamic
  }

  LineSeries {
    id: liness
    name: "LineSeries"
    axisX: xAxis
    ...
  }
}

You can take a look at the documentation to learn more about the different types of axes available.
